column2: Operation BREAKTHROUGH is a HUD research and development program to modernize the housing industry and demonstrate industrialized housing systems on nine prototype sites across eight areas of the nation, including Indianapolis, Jersey City, Kalamazoo, Macon, Memphis, Sacramento, St. Louis, Seattle, and King County, Washington. HUD considered alternatives such as no program, a purely technological program, varying the number and character of demonstration sites, and limiting demonstrations to a single housing system per site, but rejected them in favor of the broader demonstration approach. Potential environmental impacts include changes in storm runoff, visual effects of land use change, impacts on community services, and noise, with site-specific mitigations such as earthen berms, holding basins, and a siphon system, plus a total energy plant at Jersey City projected to use about half the fuel of conventional alternatives. Federal agencies including EPA, Interior, Agriculture, and FPC submitted comments, with EPA requesting separate impact statements for each site and Agriculture warning about repeating past land-use mistakes.

column2: The nine prototype sites span eight areas including Indianapolis, Jersey City, Kalamazoo, Macon, Memphis, Sacramento, St. Louis, Seattle, and King County, Washington. Site characteristics range from central city urban renewal properties to suburban neighborhoods, providing housing opportunities for a wide range of income levels. Specific sites address local concerns such as overcrowded schools in Jersey City and noise from major roadways in Memphis.

column2: Four alternatives were considered: no program, a program directed only at housing technology, different number and character of demonstration sites, and a different site design philosophy such as one system per site. The 'no program' option was rejected because the housing problem is too critical, and a purely technological program was deemed unable to overcome institutional constraints. Additional technological alternatives included conventional electrical service versus total energy systems and the emerging fuel cell technology, which Pratt and Whitney did not recommend for current demonstration use.

column2: Potential adverse impacts include changes in storm runoff, visual effects of land use change, impacts on community services, and possible effects on local property values. Site-specific mitigations include earthen berms for noise at Memphis, holding basins to reduce flooding at Indianapolis, and a siphon system to prevent eutrophication of the Macon lake. The total energy plant at Jersey City is projected to use about half the fuel of conventional alternatives with lower thermal and air pollution, and HUD has adopted noise abatement policies prohibiting support to new construction on sites with unacceptable noise exposures.
